cues.text: Trani, on Italy's Adriatic coast, preserves one of the oldest Eucharistic accounts in the country, traditionally dated to the eleventh century.
Medieval sources hold that a non-Christian woman obtained a consecrated host under false pretenses.
She subjected it to fire to test or disprove the Church's teaching on the Real Presence, and it turned visibly into bleeding flesh rather than being consumed.
According to the devotional accounts that survive, most committed to writing centuries after the event's traditional date, the host was thrown into boiling oil in a private home.
It is said to have bled so profusely that it spread through the house, drawing neighbors who alerted the local clergy.
The consecrated remains were carried to the town's churches in procession, and a chapel and later a silver reliquary were established to house them, drawing pilgrims for centuries afterward.
Because the earliest surviving written attestations date from long after the traditional eleventh-century setting, both the exact year and many narrative details cannot be fixed with confidence.
Historians of the period have documented how accounts of this kind — alleging that Jews desecrated the consecrated host — spread across medieval Europe.
They spread from the thirteenth century onward and contributed directly to expulsions, violence, and the antisemitic "blood libel" accounts.
Those accounts’ distorted echoes have never fully disappeared.

Recent Catholic commentary examining this broader catalog of medieval Eucharistic accounts has named this history directly rather than passing over it, and has called for such traditions to be presented only alongside their difficult context.
The relic remains venerated in Trani today, and the Church continues to offer devotion to it.
However, we recognize the pain and difficulties that developed in the ensuing years that lead to real animosity between Christians and their Jewish neighbors.
